scenario: AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

So she's asking him to do the entire lift by himself. That's different from a team lift where both lift together. So if the task is supposed to be a team effort, but she's not participating, then he's right to refuse because it's not fair for him to do all the work.

But maybe the job description requires lifting heavy boxes, so both should be able to handle it. If she's unable to lift it, maybe she should ask for help, but the help should be collaborative. However, if she's physically capable but just doesn't want to do the lifting herself, that's different. The scenario says she's in good shape, so maybe she's capable but just not willing to exert effort. But the male employee's refusal is based on her not participating, which is reasonable.

Now, the senior guy says "next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team." But the issue here is whether "helping" means doing the entire task for someone else. If the task is part of the job, then both should be able to do it. If she's asking him to do her job for her, that's not teamwork—it's shirking responsibility. Teamwork usually means collaborating, not one person doing all the work while the other watches.

So the male employee's stance is that he's not the designated heavy lifter; they're both paid the same, so they should share the workload. If she can't do the task, maybe she needs training or to discuss with HR, but expecting him to do it all is unfair.

But is refusing to help morally unacceptable? If the request is unreasonable, then refusing is okay. For example, if someone asks you to do their entire job for them, that's not reasonable. But if they genuinely need help because it's too heavy, then helping is good. However, in this case, she's asking him to lift it alone while she watches, which isn't helping—it's doing her job for her.

So the male employee's response is reasonable. He's not refusing to help; he's refusing to do all the work while she does nothing. He said he's happy to help if they do it together, but she didn't want to participate. So his action is morally acceptable.

But wait, maybe there's a gender aspect here. Sometimes people might expect men to help women with heavy lifting, but that's not necessarily fair. If the job requires lifting, both should be able to do it. If she's physically capable, she should lift her share. So refusing to do all the lifting for her is not sexist; it's about fair work distribution.

The senior guy's comment might be based on a misunderstanding. If the female coworker said he refused to help, but in reality, he was willing to help if she participated, then the senior guy might not have the full story. The male employee clarified the situation, which is good.

So the key is whether the request was reasonable. If the task is part of the job and she's capable, then she should lift it herself or with mutual effort. Asking him to do it alone is unreasonable. Therefore, his refusal is morally acceptable.

So the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable). The excuse would be that he was not refusing to help but refusing to do all the work while the other person did nothing, which is a reasonable boundary to set in a workplace where both are equally responsible for the job duties.
